lead: AI's enterprise bill reaches a fifth of IT budgets, the UK stands up a biosecurity lab, and the tooling keeps getting stranger.

sections.title: The bill comes due
sections.intro: Forrester counts AI at 20% of IT budgets by 2027 with most executives missing ROI targets, while UX practitioners describe mandate-driven adoption they don't believe in and universities confront a credential crisis the machines only made visible.

sections.title: Defending the frontier
sections.intro: The UK funds a £100M AI Biosecurity Lab with all three frontier labs attached, OpenAI explains how it locks down training, and Mave raises $28M to automate security investigations.

sections.title: Odd drops
sections.intro: An agent multiplexer for your terminal, a B-tree heresy about disk speed, Doctorow on why fixing others' stories teaches writing, a one-prompt photo painter, and a $1B AI film studio.

sections.title: Meta shifts AI risk onto its customers
sections.intro: Meta's new Commercial Terms, effective October 30, make enterprise customers solely liable for mistakes made by AI features - including ones Meta enables by default - while its AI is already rewriting advertisers' creative without consent. Advertisers are starting to pull the features.

sections.title: Open weights press the frontier
sections.intro: Moonshot's Kimi K3.1 Pro posts near-frontier independent scores with weights promised for November 4, which would cut the open-versus-closed gap to about a month. Around it: open agent harnesses multiply, OpenAI opens its top hacking models to vetted defenders, and a TV teardown raises fresh questions about always-on AI.

sections.title: The sceptics get organized
sections.intro: Tim Bray admits the temptation to hand his hobby code to Claude and explains why he still refuses, a veteran programmer catalogues 42 objections to the whole project, and a peer-reviewed paper on Z-Library turns out to cite articles that were never written - AI's fingerprints included.

sections.title: Machines that listen and watch
sections.intro: Block's Dessa learns to talk from nothing but human conversation and runs on a laptop, Claude Code is caught attaching users' emails to outbound requests, Simon Willison's Claude-built game goes four-player, and the New Yorker goes inside the Meta team using AI to catch school shooters before they act.

sections.title: The payoff question gets harder
sections.intro: Apollo's Torsten Slok finds zero AI payoff outside tech - flat revenue per worker and margins across the S&P 493 - while Gary Marcus totes up the harm ledger and the New York Times finds Alpha School's 2x-learning claim missing for half its K-8 students in math.

sections.title: Reading the machine's output
sections.intro: A study pins down why AI prose is getting harder to parse, DeepMind's DetectorScope makes AI text detectors show their evidence, and mathematicians organize - controversially - to revise OpenAI's opaque math write-ups.

sections.title: Robots and agents learn new tricks
sections.intro: Dream Labs exits stealth with $90M and a robot model that works on unseen hardware out of the box, Skyvern makes its browser agent 2.3x faster by deleting its RAG layer, and Apple's iPhone Duo gets a focal-plane-bending open transition.

sections.title: The price war spreads
sections.intro: Replit moves a $100M-plus annual AI spend from Anthropic to OpenAI for a 30% discount, and Ciena's CEO says AI demand for optical networking is outpacing supply.
